newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian premier warns rebel leader of attack.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian premier warns rebel leader of attack.

text.p: Cambodia's co-Prime Minister Hun Sen warned on Thursday that nominal Khmer Rouge guerrilla leader Khieu Samphan would be attacked if he returned to the capital Phnom Penh.
Hun Sen's warning came as members of co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh's party said a peace deal with the Khmer Rouge was imminent and Khieu Samphan would be allowed to enter politics.

The Khmer Rouge, responsible for the death of more than one million people during their 1975-1979 "killing fields" rule, has been decimated by government offensives, defections and splits since boycotting a 1993 election.
But even as the rebels lost military might, they have gained political muscle as the two feuding premiers have vied to win the guerrillas over to their respective ranks.

But Hun Sen said Khieu Samphan would not be welcome. He cited an incident in 1991 when Khieu Samphan was attacked and nearly lynched by a mob when he returned to Phnom Penh under the terms of an international peace treaty ending years of war.
Government security officials rescued him and he was taken, bleeding from a head wound, to Phnom Penh airport and put on a flight to Bangkok hours after arriving in the Cambodian capital.
"The people will chase him and hack him (with knives)," Hun Sen told a crowd in the southeastern province of Prey Veng.
"He returned in 1991, we tried hard to protect him but his head was broken. If he comes this time, he can't, he will be in for it."
Khieu Samphan is the official leader of a hardline Khmer Rouge faction still at war with the coalition government, though most political analysts say the notorious Pol Pot is the real leader.

A senior military commander loyal to Ranariddh told reporters this week he was concluding an agreement with the Khmer Rouge. Khieu Samphan would be allowed to enter politics while Pol Pot and two other senior commanders would go into exile and rank-and-file guerrillas would join the government side.

The agreement has not been confirmed by the government but military officials and diplomats say negotiations between Prince Ranariddh's party and the Khmer Rouge, allies during the Cambodian war in the 1980s, have been taking place.

In a guerrilla radio broadcast last month, Khieu Samphan said he would support an alliance formed by Ranariddh. Political analysts say Hun Sen is keen to prevent any such agreement in the run-up to next year's election.
In a separate development, veteran politician Pen Sovann said on Thursday he was forming a political party, the Cambodian National Supporting Party, to contest the 1998 election.
He told a news conference that for the time being he would not ally himself with either of the rival premiers.
